rashi:a1.1: And service vessels: that is, he did not need service vessels.
rashi:a1.2: And vessels of an asheira: he sacrificed with the vessels of the asheira, those same vessels that had served the asheira he used there.
rashi:a1.3: And with the wood of an asheira: he burned it [the offering], as it is written there: “And the asheira that is by it you shall cut down” [Judges 6:25].
gershom:a1.1: And with the wood of an asheira: he burned it [the offering].
gershom:a2.1: And set-aside and worshipped: [Gideon’s bull] was [both]. But in general, any animal set aside without further specification for idol worship is set-aside and prohibited.
rashi:a2.1: From where is set-aside derived in the Torah: it initially enters our mind that this is what he means: From where do we learn that a person must set aside his offering for Heaven, and not sacrifice it immediately when he has consecrated it?
rashi:a2.2: Safeguarding: for the purposes of the Most High.
tosafot:a2.1: From where is set-aside (prohibited) in the Torah: it initially enters our mind that this is what he means: From where do we learn that one must set aside the offering for the sake of sacrifice to the Most High before it is sacrificed? And he concludes that he means: From where do we learn that it is forbidden to sacrifice an animal that was set aside for idol worship? And this is somewhat difficult, since we derive this from many other verses; he should have said: This tanna brings it from here.
gershom:a3.1: From where is set-aside derived in the Torah: that one must set it aside and safeguard it before it is sacrificed, as it is written: “You shall safeguard to sacrifice to Me.”
gershom:a4.1: Anything for which they provide safeguarding: [before it is sacrificed], (to fatten it).
rashi:a3.1: A hungry lamb [imra detzoma]: a hungry lamb that was never safeguarded, and they paid no attention to it.
rashi:a3.2: For Me, and not for another master: for this is what I meant: that an animal set aside for idol worship is prohibited by Torah law is derived from here.
gershom:a5.1: If that is so, one who brought a hungry lamb and did not safeguard it: that is, if he sacrificed a lean lamb for which no safeguarding was done, since it was not fattened, would it also be prohibited?
gershom:a6.1: He said to him: I am speaking of “You shall safeguard it to sacrifice to Me in its due season”: anything that is set aside for the Most High, and not for another master.
rashi:a4.1: Until they work with it: until they do some work with it for the sake of idol worship, or pulling a wagon, or anything that is forbidden; but before that, it is not prohibited. Another version: set-aside is prohibited only until they do something with it, some work for the needs of the priests of idol worship; but once they have done some work with it, it is not prohibited, since they will no longer sacrifice it. [The text has here “and all the more so”; Tosafot, quoting this Rashi, reads “so I heard.”] And this version seems to me the main one, since it teaches “only until they work with it.” According to the first version it should not have taught “only”; it should have taught: Set-aside is not prohibited until they work with it. And the first version I did not hear [from my teachers].
tosafot:a4.1: Only until they work, etc.: Rashi explained: until they do some work with it for the sake of idol worship, or pulling a wagon, or anything forbidden; but before that they are not prohibited. Another version: until they do some work with it for the needs of the priests; but once they have done some work with it for the needs of the priests, it is not prohibited, since they will no longer sacrifice it. So I heard. And this version seems to me the main one, since it teaches “only until they work, etc.”; according to the first version he could have taught: Set-aside is prohibited [only] once they work with it. And the first version I did not hear. [This is] Rashi’s wording.
rashi:a4.2: Until they hand it over to the priests: for eating; after that they will no longer sacrifice it.
rashi:a5.1: Until they feed it vetches of idol worship: with which they fatten it for the needs of the priests, and after that they will no longer sacrifice it.
rashi:a6.1: He was from here and from there: from Babylonia and from the Land of Israel.
tosafot:a6.1: Baha was from here and from there: meaning, Baha was a Torah scholar from the Land of Israel and from Babylonia, and it was not the merit of the Land of Israel that helped him.
gershom:a7.1: Only until they perform an action upon it for the sake of idol worship: that is, either shearing or labor.
gershom:a8.1: Baha knows: that is, Baha already knew how to explain the teaching, and what helped him was that he went up there, for the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise. Rav Naḥman [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the printed Gemara has Rav Yitzḥak] said to him: Baha certainly knew how to answer, for he was from here and from there, and he studied both in Babylonia and in the Land of Israel.
rashi:a8.1: From where are these matters derived: that they are permitted for an ordinary person to eat.
tosafot:a8.1: From where are these matters derived, that set-aside and worshipped are permitted to an ordinary person: this is puzzling. From where would one come to prohibit them to an ordinary person? Even for the Most High they would not be prohibited were it not for those verses above; from where would one come to prohibit them to an ordinary person? And the Ri says: since he derives from a verse that they are prohibited for the Most High, let us derive from it that they are prohibited to an ordinary person as well. And if it is difficult: if so, what is the answer “If it enters your mind that they are prohibited to an ordinary person, why do I need a verse to exclude them from the Most High?” They would be prohibited to an ordinary person only by virtue of the verse about the Most High! One may say that this is what he means: If it enters your mind that we derive a prohibition for an ordinary person from a verse from which we learn a prohibition for the Most High, why do I need the prohibition to be written with regard to offerings? Let it be written with regard to the ordinary person, and we would automatically know that it is prohibited for the Most High from “the well-watered pastures of Israel,” from what is permitted to Israel.
gershom:a9.1: From where are these matters derived: that they are permitted to eat, since a verse was needed to exclude them. “From the well-watered pastures of Israel” means: from what is permitted to Israel shall be fit to be sacrificed. That is, these, even though they are permitted to eat, are prohibited to the Most High, for it is written “from the herd and from the flock” to exclude set-aside and worshipped.
rashi:a9.1: From the well-watered pastures of Israel: it is written with regard to offerings, in Ezekiel’s [account of the] Temple. It implies: from what is permitted for Israel to eat, bring an offering.
rashi:a9.2: And if it enters your mind: that set-aside and worshipped are prohibited to an ordinary person, why do I need those verses above, “from the herd” to exclude the worshipped, “from the flock” to exclude the set-aside? It would be derived from “the well-watered pastures of Israel,” since once something is prohibited to an ordinary person, it is prohibited to the Most High.
gershom:a10.1: For if it enters your mind that they are prohibited to an ordinary person: to eat, then why do I need the verse “from the herd and from the flock” to exclude them? Derive it from “the well-watered pastures,” from what is permitted to Israel! Rather, learn from this that the verse was needed to exclude them because they are permitted to eat. And anywhere, etc.
gershom:a16.1: Another version: Granted, if you say that [set-aside and worshipped] are permitted to Israel to eat, that is why a verse, “from the herd and from the flock,” is needed to exclude them for the Most High, even though they are permitted to Israel. But if you say, etc. [This is] like the first version, but in this version it is spelled out more fully.
rashi:a11.1: “From the animal,” “from the herd and from the flock,” “of the herd” below: “If his offering is a burnt offering of the herd,” for there is no need to state it, since “from the herd” is already written above. This lower one is certainly to exclude the tereifa, and the first one is for the worshipped animal. Evidently a verse comes for the tereifa.
gershom:a11.1: When it says “of the herd” below, there is no need to state it: since it could have said: “If his offering is a burnt offering, cattle, an unblemished male shall he offer”; rather, “of” comes to exclude the tereifa.
rashi:a12.1: It was necessary: two verses; for if there were only “the well-watered pastures of Israel,” I would say it excludes one that became a tereifa and afterward was consecrated, etc.
rashi:a12.2: I would say that it should be permitted: that is why “of the herd” was necessary. But with regard to set-aside and worshipped, why do I need two verses? If he consecrated it and afterward [someone] set it aside or worshipped it, it is not prohibited, since it is not his, and a person cannot render forbidden something that is not his. Rather, since a verse was needed to exclude them for the Most High, they are certainly permitted to an ordinary person.
tosafot:a12.1: It was necessary: that is, we always learn from “the well-watered pastures of Israel” that it is prohibited to the Most High, and even so a verse was needed to exclude a tereifa where it was consecrated and afterward became a tereifa. And Rashi explained: “But with regard to set-aside and worshipped, why do I need two verses? If he consecrated it and afterward set it aside or worshipped it, it is not prohibited, since it is not his, and a person cannot render forbidden something that is not his.” End of his words. And this is not clear, for in the chapter Yotzei Dofen (Nidda 41a), with regard to an animal that copulated with a person and one that was the object of bestiality, it requires two verses, one for a consecrated animal and one for a non-sacred animal, and the case is found with offerings of lesser sanctity, according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili [who holds that they are the owner’s property]. Therefore it seems right to explain: even if such a thing can be said with set-aside and worshipped, it is fine. For in the end, from this verse, “from the herd,” to exclude the worshipped, we learn an exclusion for only one case: where it was worshipped and afterward consecrated. And if it entered your mind that they are prohibited even to an ordinary person, let it be written with regard to the ordinary person, and for the Most High we would learn from “the well-watered pastures of Israel” that it is prohibited in this case, just as is said of the tereifa, that from “the well-watered pastures of Israel” we learn the prohibition for the Most High where it became a tereifa and afterward was consecrated. Rather, learn from the fact that it is written in the passage of offerings that it is permitted to an ordinary person. And in the chapter Yotzei Dofen (Nidda 41a) it requires another verse for the worshipped animal itself, for the Most High, where it was consecrated and afterward worshipped: that if it was brought up onto the altar, it is taken down.
gershom:a12.1: It was necessary: to exclude the tereifa, and it could not be derived from “the well-watered pastures of Israel,” for it might enter your mind that this applies only where it became a tereifa and afterward was consecrated, since when he consecrated it, it was not permitted to Israel. But if he consecrated it and afterward it became a tereifa, I would say it is permitted to the Most High, since at the time he consecrated it, it was permitted to Israel. That is why “of the herd” was necessary, to exclude the tereifa.
rashi:a13.1: Which cannot pass: for example, its legs were cut off from the knee upward. And [the Gemara asks whether] it is from here that [the case where] it became a tereifa and afterward was consecrated is derived.
gershom:a13.1: But isn’t it derived from here: [the case where] he consecrated it and afterward it became a tereifa is derived from here, “excluding a tereifa, which cannot pass.” That is, even though before then it was not a tereifa, but only after it entered the pen did it become a tereifa, its leg having broken above the knee, even so it does not pass. So too here, even though it became a tereifa only after he consecrated it, it is not sacrificed.
rashi:a14.1: It was necessary: all three verses. For if there were only “the well-watered pastures of Israel,” I would say: specifically where it was born a tereifa, similar to orla and diverse kinds in a vineyard, which are derived from that verse. For at its beginning is written “out of two hundred,” and we say in Pesaḥim (48a): “From what remains of two hundred left in the pit”: from here [we learn that] orla and diverse kinds of the vineyard are nullified in two hundred. And just as orla never had a period of fitness, so too for the tereifa we would derive from it only one that was born a tereifa. That is why “whatsoever passes” was necessary, for one that became a tereifa after its birth and was afterward consecrated; and “of the herd” comes for one that was consecrated and afterward became a tereifa.
gershom:a14.1: That too was necessary: “whatsoever passes”; and all three were necessary. For if there were only “the well-watered pastures of Israel,” I would say this applies only where it never had a period of fitness, like orla and diverse kinds of the vineyard. And what are the circumstances? For example, where it was born a tereifa from its mother’s womb: that one is prohibited, since it never had a period of fitness. But here, where it had a period of fitness, since it emerged, etc.
gershom:a15.1: I would say that it should be permitted: that is why “of the herd” is written [the printed text has a marginal suggestion: perhaps read “that even so it is prohibited”], and it is left over. “Whatsoever passes” is left over for the case where he consecrated it and afterward it became a tereifa: that it is not sacrificed.
rashi:a15.1: Mishna: the dispute of Rabbi [so Rashi’s text; the printed mishna has Rabbi Meir] and the Rabbis is explained in the Gemara.
gershom:a18.1: Another version: what are the circumstances? If it is, etc.: it explains as in the first version.
rashi:a17.1: Gemara: where she takes two [Rashi’s text reads “two”; the printed Gemara has “one” and “one hundred”]: and he had stipulated with her for only one, and gave her two; and it teaches us that he increased her payment, and all of them are payment (and not that one is a gift), since the one he stipulated with her draws [the others into its status].
gershom:a17.1: It is necessary only where she takes one fee and he gave her one hundred: it might enter your mind to say that he gave her the others as a gift, and they should be permitted. It teaches us that they are prohibited, since they all come by force of the payment, for he gave them to her for the sake of the transgression.
gershom:a19.1: Rather, this is what it teaches: he gave her [an animal] without specification; her payment is permitted, since one can say that he gave it to her as a gift.
rashi:a19.1: Let the status of payment take effect upon it retroactively: since at the time of intercourse the lamb is still extant, and since he engages in intercourse with her for the fee of that lamb, wherever it is, the status of payment takes effect upon it. Granted, where he engaged in intercourse with her and afterward gave her a lamb, one can say that since he did not designate it at the time of intercourse it is not prohibited, as it is a mere gift.
gershom:a20.1: Rabbi Elazar said: where she first sacrificed it, before he engaged in intercourse with her; that is why her payment is permitted.
rashi:b1.1: Where she first sacrificed it: before intercourse.
gershom:b1.1: What are the circumstances? If he transferred it to her: at the time he gave it to her.
gershom:b2.1: It is obvious: that even had she not first sacrificed it, it would be permitted, since the status of payment does not take effect upon it.
gershom:b3.1: For until then he had not engaged in intercourse with her: when he gave it to her.
gershom:b4.1: Rather, where he said to her: It shall not be acquired by you until the time of intercourse, and she went ahead and sacrificed it. Another version: since he did not transfer it to her, how can she sacrifice it? “And a man,” etc. [Leviticus 27:14].
rashi:b3.1: And if you need it, take it from now: therefore it is in her possession and she can sacrifice it. And since he said to her: It shall not be acquired by you until the time of intercourse, it was necessary to teach us that it is permitted if she first sacrificed it, for it might enter your mind that it is payment.
gershom:b5.1: It is necessary only where he said to her: It shall not be acquired by you until the time of intercourse, and if you need it before then, either to eat or to sacrifice, it shall be acquired by you from now. For even though, when he said to her “it shall not be acquired by you,” he certainly gave it as payment, even so, since he said to her “if you need it, it shall be acquired by you from now,” it is now in her possession and she can sacrifice it. If she first sacrificed it, it is permitted.
gershom:b6.1: Another version: if you need it, take it out for whatever you wish.
rashi:b5.1: He raises the statement of Rabbi Elazar itself as a dilemma: meaning, was it obvious to Rabbi Elazar that if she sacrificed it, yes [it is permitted], but if she consecrated it, no? Or perhaps “she sacrificed it” was obvious to him, while “she consecrated it” was uncertain to him? It stands unresolved.
rashi:b6.1: A declaration to the Most High: and he cannot retract, as though he had transferred it to an ordinary person.
rashi:b8.1: For this lamb: since he gave it at the time of intercourse, the status of payment takes effect upon it immediately.
rashi:b8.2: A lamb, without specification: what he sends her afterward is a mere gift, and payment is only what was designated at the time of intercourse.
gershom:b7.1: Where he said to her: Engage in intercourse with me for this lamb: even if he did not give it to her until three years later [the printed Gemara: twelve months], it is prohibited. But where he said, Engage in intercourse with me for a lamb, without specification, and he gave it to her after he had engaged in intercourse with her, it is permitted, since one can say that this lamb, since he did not designate it for her, perhaps he gave it to her as a gift. And when he said, for this lamb, why is it prohibited? It lacks pulling, since the prostitute did not pull it and did not acquire it; let it be like when he said “for a lamb” without specification. We are dealing with a gentile prostitute, who does not acquire by pulling. Another version: since a gentile woman acquires with money, here too, since he said to her “for this lamb” and engaged in intercourse with her, she acquired it through her intercourse even though she did not pull it: by the law of gentiles, who acquire with money that they give without pulling, so too this one acquired it through the intercourse.
gershom:b8.1: And if you wish, say: even a Jewish prostitute. And it is found that from the time he engaged in intercourse with her she acquired it, when he said “for this lamb,” for example, where they stationed it in her courtyard, for a person’s courtyard acquires for him.
tosafot:b9.1: Such as where it is standing in her courtyard: this implies that we find payment only in such a case, where it is standing in her courtyard. If so, there is a difficulty with what is said in Merubbe (Bava Kamma 70b) with regard to payment: the Torah prohibited payment even where he engaged in intercourse with his mother, where he is liable to death [and so exempt from monetary payment], since if she summoned him before us to judgment we would not say to him: Go, give it to her, for he is liable with his life. Now, since we find payment only where it is standing in her courtyard, how does it apply to say “Go, give it to her”? She has already seized it! And the Ri explained: since, had she not been in possession of it, we would not say to him “Go, give it to her,” then even though she now acquires it by virtue of her courtyard, we would not call it payment, were it not for the reason explained there: since he gives it to her in order to fulfill his obligation in the eyes of Heaven, it is payment. And my teacher the Ramar explained that we need not say this. The reason the Gemara establishes it here as standing in her courtyard is that it is hard to find [a case of] “he engaged in intercourse with her and afterward gave her”; but if he transferred it to her with a kinyan sudar [acquisition by means of a cloth]: When you have intercourse with me, this lamb shall be acquired by you, it is acquired wherever it is. And with this the passage in Merubbe is fine: if she summoned him before us to judgment, we would not say to him, Go, give it to her.
rashi:b10.1: But he gave it to her at the outset: since it is standing in her courtyard, she acquires it immediately at the time of intercourse. So why does it call it “and afterward he gave”? And furthermore, it is obvious that it is prohibited.
gershom:b9.1: If so, he gave it to her at the outset, before intercourse, when they stationed it in her courtyard. So why is it speaking of “he engaged in intercourse with her and afterward gave her”?
rashi:b10.2: By such and such a day I will pay you such and such, and if I do not pay: therefore, when the day arrives and he has not given her money, it becomes clear [that it was hers at the time] of intercourse. But it is [called given] afterward, since it was not hers until such and such a day arrived; and it was necessary to teach us that it is prohibited.
gershom:b10.1: Rather, where he made it for her: this lamb, a security [apotiki], and said to her: If by such and such a day I give you money for your payment, well and good; and if not, take the whole lamb as your payment. Therefore, since he made it a security for her, she acquired it, but not fully until the time passes; therefore it too is like “he engaged in intercourse with her and afterward gave her.”
gershom:b11.1: Another version: where it is established as standing in [her] courtyard, he gave it to her and afterward engaged in intercourse with her. Rather, for example, where a shepherd handed it over to her by pulling, and afterward it came into his master’s hands, and he did not give it to her until after intercourse.
rashi:b11.1: The payment of a male: one who engaged in intercourse with a male and gave him payment; it is prohibited for sacrifice.
rashi:b13.1: “Abomination” is written: “For both of them are an abomination to the Lord your God.” And this too is an abomination, for the menstruating woman is written among the forbidden relations, and of all of them it is written: “All these abominations.”
gershom:b12.1: What is the reason? “For it is an abomination” is written, and his menstruating wife is an abomination, since she is written among the forbidden relations, and at the end of it is written: “For whoever shall do any of these abominations.” And according to Levi, who includes his menstruating wife: but “prostitute” is written, and his menstruating wife is not a prostitute.
gershom:b13.1: And Rav [the printed text emends to “and Rav”; in the Gemara this answer is given for Levi] holds that this “prostitute” comes for this: that the payment of a female prostitute is prohibited, but not the payment of a male prostitute; if she gave him payment, it is not prohibited for sacrifice.
rashi:b14.1: And not a male prostitute: for if she gave him payment, it is permitted.
rashi:b15.1: Who come to him through transgression: in whom there is no aspect of permission. But his menstruating wife, who is permitted to him after a time, or where he gave a prostitute a fee for her neglect, payment for the time she was idle from her work and not payment for intercourse [these are permitted].
gershom:b14.1: Or where he gave her a fee for her neglect: not payment for the transgression, but payment for her being idle at that time from her work; all of these are permitted.
rashi:b16.1: And even though there is no proof for the matter: that it should be permitted for sacrifice, there is an allusion to the matter that what she gives him is not payment, from what is written: “Thus you are contrary.”
gershom:b15.1: And even though there is no proof for the matter: there is an allusion to the matter that a prostitute’s payment is called payment, as it is said: “And in that you gave hire.” And he says that all of these are permitted.
gershom:b16.1: And Rav, this “abomination” that Levi expounds for payment to his menstruating wife, what does he do with it? He requires it, etc. He derives “abomination,” “abomination” from forbidden relations: it is written with regard to payment “for it is an abomination,” and it is written with regard to forbidden relations “of all these abominations.” Excluded is a gentile woman, whose offspring are not attributed to him, as we say: Your son from a gentile woman is not called your son, but her son.
rashi:b19.1: A gentile woman, whose offspring are not attributed to him: for the child is not called his offspring but her son, as we say in Yevamot (23a): Your son from a Jewish woman is called your son, but your son from a gentile woman is not called your son, but her son.
rashi:b21.1: What is the reason? They are derived from one another: by [the method of] ma matzinu [an analogy from what we have found].
tosafot:b21.1: And Rava says: both this and that, her payment is prohibited, and a priest who engaged in intercourse with her is flogged on account of a prostitute: this is difficult. If so, what did the court of the Hasmoneans decree? For they decreed that one who has intercourse with a gentile woman is liable on account of NaShGaZ [menstruating woman, maidservant, gentile, prostitute], yet here it says that a gentile woman is a prostitute by Torah law! One may say that Rava holds like the one who says NaShGA [menstruating woman, maidservant, gentile, married woman], but on account of a prostitute he is flogged by Torah law. And if you say: according to Abaye, who said that a priest who has intercourse with a gentile woman is not flogged on account of a prostitute, but we learned in the chapter HaBa al Yevimto (Yevamot 59b and 61a): “A prostitute is only a convert, and one who had licentious intercourse,” evidently a gentile woman is a prostitute! One may say: once she has converted, she is certainly a prostitute; but while she is still a gentile, she is not a prostitute.
gershom:b17.1: And Rava says, etc.: and a priest who has intercourse with her, even with a gentile woman, is flogged on account of a prostitute, since they are derived from one another. Just as a Jewish prostitute is by a prohibition, as it is written “he shall not profane,” so too a gentile woman by a prohibition; and just as payment to a gentile woman is prohibited, since betrothal does not take effect with her, so too payment to a Jewish prostitute is prohibited even though betrothal takes effect with her, since they are derived from one another.
tosafot:b22.1: In brief: Tosafot sets out two readings of this passage. First reading: “They raised an objection: both a prostitute and a gentile woman.” It was first thought to mean a Jewish prostitute who is already a prostitute (e.g., she had relations with one liable for karet, or is promiscuous), so that payment to her is prohibited for anyone, even one permitted to her. That would be Rava’s view and refute Abaye, who derives “abomination,” “abomination” that payment applies only where betrothal does not take effect. The Gemara asks from the last clause, a widow with a High Priest, where betrothal does take effect, and answers that it is Rabbi Elazar, for whom an unmarried man with an unmarried woman renders her a prostitute, so every act outside full marriage is payment; the Rabbis would limit payment to relations where betrothal does not take effect. Tosafot asks how Abaye knows that Rabbi Elazar does not also derive “abomination,” “abomination,” and answers that since Rabbi Elazar is stricter about a prostitute than other tanna’im, he is stricter about payment too. On “Why specifically a widow?” and “since it is the paradigm,” Tosafot quotes Rashi (the unmarried case is the paradigm, so one might think a widow already forbidden to the High Priest is not payment) and calls it hard to understand; Rabbeinu Netanel explains that the paradigm equates payment with the priest’s prohibition of a prostitute, so a widow with a High Priest, forbidden under another name and not as a prostitute, might not be payment. Second reading (in the books, as printed here): the answer “It is Rabbi Akiva, who says betrothal does not take effect with those liable for prohibitions.” Tosafot asks why the Gemara adds “and this teaches us…,” and answers: had the baraita taught only the first clause, one might err and think that a woman who is already a prostitute counts as one for payment even when hired by a man permitted to her; the last clause teaches that payment arises only from relations where betrothal does not take effect, like a widow with a High Priest, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rava’s answer (“similar to a widow… until he says: This is for you”): Rashi says that for Rava a woman who was a prostitute from the outset has prohibited payment even without specification. Tosafot finds this forced, since according to the Rabbis there is no case where payment without specification is not payment, and proposes instead: payment given to a woman who already became a prostitute (through karet relations, or a promiscuous woman) by a man with whom betrothal takes effect is payment only if he states explicitly “Here is this lamb as your payment”; this excludes Rabbi Elazar, for whom it is payment even without specification. And “where she was a prostitute from the outset” means, also according to the Rabbis, where she becomes a prostitute through that very act for which he pays (e.g., his sister, or one liable for karet): then it is payment even without specification. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b18.1: Abaye could have said to you: that is why a Jewish prostitute is likened to a gentile prostitute: just as with a [gentile] prostitute betrothal does not take effect, so too the Jewish prostitute [of the baraita].
gershom:b19.1: [It refers] to forbidden relations with whom betrothal does not take effect; but where betrothal takes effect, the payment is permitted. But the last clause of this baraita teaches: “Both a gentile prostitute, etc., for example, a widow with a High Priest, etc.” With these, betrothal takes effect and their payment is prohibited; this is difficult for Abaye.
gershom:b20.1: Abaye could have said to you: this last clause, whose is it? It is Rabbi Elazar, who said: An unmarried man, etc., not for the sake of marriage [ishut], betrothal.
